title: Serving Runtime: profiling, benchmarking, kernel scheduling & runbooks
author: Asha Patel
content:
Purpose

This page collects canonical guidance for the serving-runtime team: architecture overview, kernel selection and scheduling policies, a step-by-step profiling playbook, the canonical benchmarking harness and CI gates, recent release highlights, known issues and mitigations, and on-call runbooks. Intended readers: runtime engineers, SREs, applied ML engineers, and platform owners.

Summary (TL;DR)
- Goals: meet latency SLOs (p95/p99), maximize throughput, and minimize cost per token.
- Main levers: kernel choice, batching policy, KV-cache strategy, quantization profile, and autoscaling.
- Production targets: p95 < 120ms for chat <=512 tokens; p99 < 350ms for single-turn generation on A100 dedicated pools.

1. Architecture (concise)
- Frontend router: auth, shaping, and preliminary routing.
- Broker: per-model queues, adaptive batching, latency budgeting.
- Worker pool: GPU-backed agents running the runtime kernel, KV cache, and streamer.
- Cache: per-worker KV cache plus optional shared prefix cache for hot prompts.
- Telemetry: token-level metrics, kernel histograms, trace context.
- Control plane: model catalog, rollout policies, routing rules, and autoscaling controller.

Dataflow (short): request -> router -> broker/batch -> worker executes kernel -> update KV cache -> stream response -> emit metrics.

2. Kernel taxonomy and selection heuristics
- Kernel types: fp16/AMP, int8/quantized, fused-attn (long-context), vendor/custom fused ops.
- Selection inputs: model architecture, expected sequence length, target batch size, memory headroom, and quality constraints.
- Heuristic ordering (simplified):
  1) If certified quant profile and acceptable quality delta -> quantized kernel.
  2) If seq_len > 1024 and fused-attn available -> fused-attn.
  3) Otherwise -> fp16/AMP kernel.
- Kernels are scored by per-token latency, throughput, and memory footprint. Scores are calibrated using offline microbenchmarks and production telemetry.

Scheduling policies
- Priority classes: default, low-latency, background.
- Adaptive batch windows: broker adjusts timeouts to trade queue latency vs throughput based on SLOs.
- Work stealing: idle GPUs can pull low-priority work if it fits latency tail constraints to improve utilization.
- Fallbacks: automatic retry with next-compatible kernel on OOM or operator failure, with alerting.

3. Profiling playbook (step-by-step)
When to profile
- Sudden increase in p95/p99 for a route or model.
- Rising variance in batch sizes or unexplained memory pressure.
- Kernel errors, operator failures, or increases in kernel-level exception rates.

Minimum data to collect
- Route, model version, example prompts (sample of 10-50), batch-shape distribution, time window, pool IDs.
- Telemetry: request rate, p50/p95/p99, batch-size histogram, kernel selection history, and recent autoscaler events.

Profiling steps
1) Reproduce the workload on a staging pool with production-sampled traffic using the benchmark harness.
2) Collect system metrics: nvidia-smi (util/mem), dstat, and perf counters during the run.
3) Enable verbose kernel telemetry (operator-level timings, allocator events) for the model under test.
4) Run microbenchmarks: single-batch latency and throughput across candidate kernels and input shapes.
5) Compare traces (flame graphs/diff profiles) to identify regressions at the operator or scheduling layer.
6) Force kernels if selection differs to determine whether selection heuristics or kernel implementation is root cause.
7) For memory regressions, capture allocation traces and run OOM reproducers to observe tensor lifetimes.

Useful commands (examples)
- Run harness: ./bench/harness --model gptx-7b --prompts prompts/sample.jsonl --batch-shape 4x512 --target-pool staging-us-west-1 --profile kernel,alloc --out run-20260303.tar.gz
- GPU snapshot: nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.used,utilization.gpu --format=csv
- Kernel telemetry: runtime_cli get-kernel-trace --run-id run-20260303 --output kernel-trace.json

4. Benchmarking suite (canonical harness)
Goals
- Produce repeatable measurements for latency/throughput/cost across kernels and model variants.
- Prevent regressions: CI gates and nightly regression comparisons.

Test matrix
- Microbenchmarks: single-batch latency for sequence lengths [32,128,512,1024,2048].
- Batch scaling: throughput vs batch size sweep.
- Mixed workloads: realistic distributions of short chat and long generation.
- End-to-end tests: streaming simulations for tail-latency measurement.

Harness flags and outputs
- Flags: --model, --kernel, --prompts, --batch-shape, --duration, --target-pool, --profile.
- Outputs: p50/p95/p99 latencies, batch-size histogram, per-token decode time, GPU utilization, cost-estimate report, and kernel-selection breakdown.

CI gates
- Microbenchmark tolerances: per-model p95 regressions <= 3% unless approved.
- Nightly job compares master baseline vs branch and files regression tickets automatically when thresholds are exceeded.

5. Release highlights (recent)
v2026.02 (2026-02-20)
- Faster int8 kernel for gptx-7b (~18% per-token latency reduction at batch>=4).
- Adaptive batch window now respects per-route latency overrides.
- KV cache cleanup memory leak fixed.
- Kernel-level op histograms added for staging.

v2025.11 (2025-11-10)
- Work-stealing scheduler deployed to improve idle-GPU utilization.
- Benchmark harness added mixed-workload simulation mode.

6. Known issues and mitigations
- p99 spikes on very long-context workloads (>=2048 tokens): correlated with allocator stalls. Mitigation: route to fused-attn pools and enlarge per-worker allocation arenas. Patch scheduled for v2026.04.
- Quantized kernel quality deltas for hallucination-sensitive tasks: mitigation via canary rollouts with prompt-level quality checks and automatic fallback.
- Missing custom vendor kernels on some customer private deployments: mitigation via image validation script (see Appendix).

7. On-call runbooks (quick actions)
Alert: p99 latency > SLO for 10m on a route
1) Triage scope: check dashboards and identify affected pools.
2) Kernel distribution: runtime_cli get-route-kernel-stats --route <route> --window 10m.
3) If queue time increased: consider scaling or diverting traffic to dedicated pools.
4) If kernel failures/ooms: force-safe-kernel, mark workers draining, and rollback if needed.
5) Attach traces and profiling artifacts to the incident ticket.

OOM on worker
1) Drain worker: infra_cli drain-worker --id <id>.
2) Pull allocation trace: runtime_cli get-alloc-trace --worker <id> --last 1h.
3) Reproduce with harness in staging.
4) Escalate to kernel team with traces if reproducible.

Throughput degradation but stable latency
- Check batch-size histogram and autoscaler events; increase autoscaler sensitivity or adjust thresholds if a traffic shift is observed.

8. Ownership and contacts
- Serving-runtime team: primary owners; pager: @serving-runtime-oncall.
- Kernel team: owns kernel implementations and microbenchmarks.
- SRE: autoscaling and capacity planning.
- Applied ML: quality validation for quantized/approximated kernels.

- Ops playbook: /confluence/eng-serving-runtime/serving-runtime-ops-playbook-2026
- Benchmark dashboards: internal://dashboards/kernel-benchmarks
- Harness repo: git@redwood:infra/serving-bench.git

Appendix: sample pool config (YAML)
| name: fused-attn-pool | gpu_type: a100 | min_replicas: 2 | max_replicas: 20 | target_p95_ms: 120 | supported_kernels: [fused-attn, fp16] |

Customer image validation (quick)
1) docker run --rm -e MODEL=gptx-7b -v $(pwd):/work redwood/runtime-validator:stable /work/validate.sh
2) validate.sh runs kernel smoke tests, quantized op checks and allocator sanity checks and emits a validation report.
